title: Correlated Errors in Large Language Models

cost.compute_notes: 220 HELM scenario fetches (~7.6MB) + 247MB repo clone (3 files >50MB deleted after inspection per disk policy); 4 analysis scripts, longest run ~3min single-core pandas/stdlib

triggers: do different LLMs make the same mistakes
is a second model's opinion independent
does using a different vendor's model give me diversity
everyone screened by the same model gets rejected everywhere
should all our firms use the best model or different ones

claims.statement: Conditional on two LLMs both answering a multiple-choice question incorrectly, they select the same incorrect answer far more often than chance.
claims.scope: MMLU-style multiple-choice items, models drawn from public leaderboards (HELM, HuggingFace Open LLM Leaderboard 2), 2023-2024 model generations.

our_assessment.why: The number replicates (we measured 0.5528 on an independently rebuilt 22-model x 2918-item HELM sample). What does not survive is its interpretation as evidence of dependence between models. The uniform-over-wrong baseline assumes all distractors are equally attractive, which is false for professionally written MCQ items and false in an ability-graded way: corr(model accuracy, P(picks the modal wrong answer | wrong)) = +0.835. Two models conditionally independent given the item can produce this number. Per jo2026-subjectivity Thm 1 there is no null-free fact of the matter here, so the honest status is not-identifiable rather than refuted.

claims.statement: Error correlation is higher for pairs sharing a provider, sharing a base architecture, or having similar parameter counts; and, conditional on those, higher for pairs that are individually more accurate.
claims.scope: OLS on pair-level features; HELM, HuggingFace, Resumes.

our_assessment.why: The provider/architecture part survives our item-corrected reanalysis: same-provider pairs retain a residual (+0.066 vs +0.007 cross-provider under a leave-provider-out null), and the largest genuine residual is llama-3.1-405b/llama-3.1-70b (+0.274). Family kinship is real. The accuracy part is the problem: any null estimated from a mixed-ability population scores high-accuracy pairs as excessively correlated almost mechanically. Our anchored nulls are antisymmetric at nearly equal magnitude (weak-anchor -> strong-target +0.212, strong-anchor -> weak-target -0.206), which is the signature of a capability-gap artifact rather than kinship.

claims.statement: An LLM used as a judge systematically inflates the measured accuracy of models less accurate than itself and deflates that of models more accurate than itself, with additional inflation for models from its own provider or family.
claims.scope: HELM and HuggingFace MMLU; each of ~15 models used in turn as judge.

our_assessment.why: Mechanically sound and does not depend on the disputed null: a judge cannot reward a correct answer it would not itself have produced, so the deflation arm is near-tautological, and the inflation arm follows directly from shared errors being scored as correct. The same-provider extra inflation extends self-preferencing (Panickssery et al. 2024) from a model to a family. This is the most directly actionable result in the paper and the least cited.

claims.statement: In a simulated labour market, LLM-based screening produces substantial systemic exclusion even when every firm independently uses a different LLM; and firm welfare is maximised by all firms using the same best model rather than diversifying.
claims.scope: 1800 resume-job pairs, 450 human-labelled, 20 LLMs, deferred-acceptance stable matching, 1500 simulated markets.

our_assessment.why: We did not re-run the market simulations. Recorded because it is the half of the paper that does not depend on the contested correlation statistic, and because the applicant-welfare result runs OPPOSITE to the firm-welfare result (monoculture is best for firms, worst for applicants) which is the kind of finding that gets dropped in citation. The data artifact for this half (data/final.csv, 63MB) was inspected and deleted under our >50MB policy; restorable via git checkout.

relations.why: Takes the component-sharing hypothesis and outcome-homogenization framing and tests it at leaderboard scale on LLMs rather than on census fairness benchmarks.
We rebuilt the item-level data from upstream after the repo's raw file proved dangling, and located a mechanism (competence concentrates errors) that reinterprets c1.
Nikhil Garg authors both. jo2026 is substantially a self-correction, which is why it deserves more weight than an adversarial critique would.

open_questions: Does the ability-graded concentration of errors persist in open-ended generation, where there is no enumerated distractor set? The whole monoculture literature is built on multiple choice, and our agents do not work in multiple choice.

The market results (c4) do not depend on the contested statistic and were never re-run by us. If firm welfare really is maximised by monoculture while applicant welfare is minimised, that is the policy-relevant finding and it is under-argued relative to the correlation headline.
Their Appendix B/C report alternate correlation measures (overall agreement, agreement-when-either-wrong). Do those move under an item-difficulty null in the same direction? Cheap to check with a3.

Is the deposited model_correlations.csv the exact run behind the paper, or a later regeneration? Four printed numbers miss in the last digit, coherently and in one direction. The item-level file that would settle it is the dead LFS object, so the question is undecidable from the deposit -- which is itself the cleanest example this corpus has that artifact PRESENCE and artifact SUFFICIENCY FOR REANALYSIS are different properties.
